C2.1.q: What does a low-pass filter do to a sound?
options: Turns down everything below the cutoff
Turns down everything above the cutoff
Keeps only a thin slice around the cutoff
Turns the whole sound down by the same amount
C2.1.why: A low-pass filter lets the lows pass and turns down what is above the cutoff.

C2.1.q: You slowly lower the cutoff on a bright, buzzy note. What do you hear?
options: The note drops lower in pitch
The lowest harmonics vanish first
The buzz fades from the top down
The note gets louder and harsher
C2.1.why: Lowering the cutoff removes harmonics from the top, one after another, so the note goes from buzzy to rounded to dull.

C2.1.q: The low-pass curve is flat on the left and falls away on the right. What does that tell you?
options: Highs get through and lows are turned down
The note gets quieter the longer it sounds
The note sounds lower when you play higher keys
Lows get through and highs are turned down
C2.1.why: The curve shows what gets through at each frequency: flat where sound passes, falling where it is turned down.

C2.2.q: Where does resonance add its boost?
options: In a narrow band right at the cutoff
At the very lowest frequencies only
Evenly across the whole sound
In a wide band far above the cutoff
C2.2.why: Resonance boosts a narrow band right at the cutoff, seen as a bump on the curve.

C2.2.q: Why does a cutoff sweep with resonance whistle or squelch instead of plainly fading?
options: The note you play changes pitch during the sweep
The whole sound gets louder as you sweep
The peak pushes forward one harmonic after another
The filter switches shape as the cutoff moves
C2.2.why: Whatever harmonic sits under the bump is pushed forward, so the sweep picks out harmonics one by one.

C2.2.q: You push resonance very high. What happens to the rest of the sound on this synth?
options: It gets louder along with the peak
It is turned down, so the body thins
It stays exactly as loud as before
It gets brighter from the top down
C2.2.why: On this synth the rest of the sound is turned down as the peak grows, so there is less body.

C2.3.q: You want to drain a note's weight and leave only the fizzy top. Which shape do you pick?
options: Low-pass
Band-pass
Notch
High-pass
C2.3.why: High-pass keeps what is above the cutoff, so raising it takes the weight away from the bottom up.

C2.3.q: A sound is small and boxy, like a voice on a telephone. Which shape gives that?
options: Notch, which removes a slice
Low-pass, which keeps the lows
Band-pass, which keeps a slice
High-pass, which keeps the highs
C2.3.why: Band-pass keeps only a slice around the cutoff, which gives a small, boxy sound.

C2.3.q: On a band-pass filter, what does raising resonance do?
options: Makes the slice narrower
Makes the slice wider
Moves the slice higher up
Turns the slice into a notch
C2.3.why: On band-pass and notch, resonance sets how narrow the slice is.

C2.4.q: What does a filter's slope describe?
options: Where the cutoff sits in the sound
How big the boost at the cutoff is
How fast it turns things down past the cutoff
How loud the sound is before the filter
C2.4.why: Slope is how quickly the filter turns things down the further past the cutoff they are.

C2.4.q: On the steep slope, how far down is a harmonic one octave above the cutoff?
options: 12 dB down
24 dB down
Not turned down at all
Removed completely
C2.4.why: The steep slope is 24 decibels per octave; the gentle one is 12.

C2.4.q: You switch from gentle to steep without touching the cutoff. What changes?
options: The sound gets brighter
The note drops in pitch
Nothing, until the cutoff moves
The sound gets darker
C2.4.why: At the same cutoff a steeper slope turns the upper harmonics down more, so it sounds darker.

C2.5.q: Why does drive make a sound thicker and grittier?
options: It lowers the cutoff of the filter
Squashing the wave's peaks adds harmonics
It adds a boost right at the cutoff
It removes the highest harmonics first
C2.5.why: Drive squashes the wave's peaks flat, and changing a wave's shape adds harmonics.

C2.5.q: Drive is high. What happens to the grit when you close the filter?
options: The filter tames it: warm and thick
It gets harsher than with the filter open
It stays the same, as drive comes after the filter
It disappears, leaving a clean tone
C2.5.why: The squashing happens before the filter, so the filter smooths the new harmonics when it closes.

C2.5.q: With drive up, one key plays two notes instead of one. What do you hear?
options: A cleaner sound than one note gave
The same clear tone, only louder
A growl, rougher than either note alone
A quieter sound, as the notes cancel
C2.5.why: Single notes stay clear under drive, but two notes together turn rough.

C2.6.q: With no key tracking, why can a high note sound duller than a low one?
options: High notes are always quieter than low notes
The filter switches itself off for high notes
The cutoff climbs too far on high notes
The fixed cutoff sits below the high note's harmonics
C2.6.why: The cutoff stays at one frequency while the note moves up past it, so the high note loses its harmonics.

options: Moves the cutoff with the key you play
Moves the pitch with the cutoff you set
Makes high keys louder than low keys
Adds a boost at the cutoff for each key
C2.6.why: Key tracking moves the cutoff up and down with the key you play.

C2.6.q: At 100% key tracking, what stays the same from note to note?
options: The frequency of the cutoff
The brightness of each note
The pitch that each key plays
The length of each note
C2.6.why: At 100% the cutoff moves as far as the pitch does, so every note keeps the same brightness.

C2.7.q: What happens when noise goes through a filter with very high resonance?
options: The noise gets louder but stays pitchless
The noise is removed, leaving silence
The filter rings, and you hear a whistle
The noise turns smooth and dull
C2.7.why: At high resonance the filter rings at its cutoff, and noise keeps that ringing going.

C2.7.q: How do you change the pitch of the filter's whistle?
options: Move the cutoff
Change the level of the noise
Turn the resonance down a little
Change the level of oscillator A
C2.7.why: The whistle's pitch is the cutoff frequency, so moving the cutoff moves the pitch.

C2.7.q: What lets you play the filter's whistle as a tune from the keys?
options: Key tracking at zero
Resonance at zero
Oscillator A at full level
Key tracking at 100%
C2.7.why: With full key tracking the cutoff follows the keys, so the whistle moves in step with them.

C2.C.q: When matching a hidden filtered sound, what should you ask first?
options: Whether it is clean or gritty
What is missing: top, bottom or both
Whether it falls away gently or sharply
Whether there is a whistle in it
C2.C.why: Asking what is missing first gives you the filter type and roughly where the cutoff is.

C2.C.q: The hidden sound has a whistle or edge at one frequency. Which setting does that point to?
options: Drive
Slope
Resonance
Filter type
C2.C.why: A whistle or edge at one spot is resonance; grit and squashing is drive.

C2.C.q: What is the best way to compare your sound with the target?
options: Switch quickly between the two
Listen to the target for a long time
Read the target's numbers from the app
Change every setting before listening again
C2.C.why: Quick switching between the target and your sound tells you more than long listening.

C3.1.q: Which of the four envelope stages is a level, not a time?
options: Attack
Decay
Release
Sustain
C3.1.why: Attack, decay and release are times; sustain is the level the note stays at while held.

C3.1.q: You raise Release to about one second. When do you hear the difference?
options: While the key is held down
After you let go of the key
At the very start of the note
Only when sustain is at zero
C3.1.why: Release is how long the note takes to fade after you let go, so it only matters then.

C3.1.q: Sustain is at 0 with a short decay. You hold a key. What do you hear?
options: A pluck that dies away while you hold
A note that fades in slowly
A steady note for as long as you hold
A note that starts only when you let go
C3.1.why: With no sustain the note falls to silence by itself, which is a pluck.

C3.2.q: Which settings give an organ shape?
options: No attack, no sustain, a short decay
Long attack, high sustain, long release
No attack, full sustain, no release
Long attack, no sustain, no release
C3.2.why: An organ switches on and off at once and stays at full level in between.

C3.2.q: On a pluck, what sets how long the note lasts?
options: The sustain level
The decay time
The attack time
How long you hold the key
C3.2.why: A pluck has no sustain, so it dies away by itself and the decay sets its length.

C3.2.q: The oscillators stay the same. What turns an organ sound into a pad?
options: It starts at once and dies away
It switches on and off like a light
It stops as soon as the key is let go
It swells in and fades out slowly
C3.2.why: A pad has a slow attack, high sustain and slow release, so it swells in and fades out.

C3.3.q: What does Hold do to a note?
options: Keeps it at full level for a time after the attack
Keeps it ringing for a time after you let go
Sets the level it rests at while the key is held
Makes it take longer to reach full level
C3.3.why: Hold keeps the note at full level after the attack, before the decay begins.

C3.3.q: You switch Fall from Eased to Sharp and leave the decay time alone. How does the note seem?
options: Longer and flatter, then a sudden stop
Exactly as long as it was before
Much shorter, with a snappy front
Slower to reach full level
C3.3.why: The decay time is the same, but a sharp fall loses most of its level almost at once, so it seems shorter.

C3.3.q: Which fall shape sounds mechanical instead of plucked or struck?
options: Eased
Straight
Sharp
Sharp with Hold added
C3.3.why: A straight fall loses level at an even rate, which sounds mechanical; eased and sharp sound struck or plucked.

C3.4.q: Envelope 2 is sent to the cutoff with a positive amount. What does each note do?
options: Starts quiet, then gets louder
Starts high in pitch, then drops
Stays at one steady brightness
Starts bright, then closes down
C3.4.why: The envelope pushes the cutoff up at the start of each note and lets it fall back.

C3.4.q: The bright start of each note is over too quickly. Which Envelope 2 control do you raise?
options: Decay
Amount
Sends to
Cutoff
C3.4.why: Decay sets how long the change takes; amount sets how far the envelope pushes.

C3.4.q: What does turning Amount below zero do?
options: Each note starts even brighter than before
The envelope stops moving the cutoff
Each note starts muffled and opens up
Each note fades in from silence
C3.4.why: A negative amount turns the shape upside down, so the cutoff starts low and rises.

C3.5.q: What do you hear when an envelope is sent to an oscillator's pitch?
options: Each note gets brighter, then duller
Each note slides into place
Each note fades in slowly
Each note rings on after you let go
C3.5.why: An envelope on pitch makes each note start away from its real pitch and slide into place.

C3.5.q: You want a pitch envelope to sound like an impact, not a slide. What do you set?
options: A large amount and a short decay
A small amount and a long decay
A large amount and a long decay
A small amount and no decay at all
C3.5.why: Fast and far reads as an impact; slow and slight reads as a scoop.

C3.5.q: Why send the pitch envelope to Osc B only and leave Osc A alone?
options: To make both oscillators fall together
To make the whole note scoop up from below
To stop Osc A from sounding at the start
To add a knock on top of a steady tone
C3.5.why: A stays steady while B falls on top of it, which adds a knock at the front of the sound.

C3.6.q: Does the envelope move the cutoff differently on a high-pass than on a low-pass?
options: Yes: on a high-pass it pushes down first
Yes: on a high-pass the cutoff stays still
No: it pushes up then falls on both
Yes: on a high-pass it only rises
C3.6.why: The envelope moves the cutoff the same way on every shape; what you hear depends on which side the filter keeps.

C3.6.q: On a high-pass, the cutoff falls during each note. What do you hear?
options: A bright start that closes down
A thin start, then the low end arrives
A full start that thins out
A steady tone with no change
C3.6.why: On a high-pass a falling cutoff lets the low end back in, so the body of the note arrives late.

C3.6.q: On a band-pass with a falling cutoff, what does each note sound like?
options: A vowel changing as a slice slides down
The body of the note arriving late
Brightness draining away from the top
A note slowly fading in from silence
C3.6.why: On a band-pass the slice that gets through slides downward, which sounds like a vowel changing.

C3.C.q: How should you listen to a hidden sound's shape in time?
options: The whole note as one impression
Only the first instant of the note
Only what happens after you let go
Start, middle and end, each separately
C3.C.why: Listening to the start, the middle and the end separately tells you how the note begins, settles and ends.

C3.C.q: A hidden sound changes brightness during each note. What is causing it?
options: A long release on the loudness envelope
A slow attack on the loudness envelope
An envelope sent to the filter
A higher sustain level on the note
C3.C.why: A change in brightness during the note is an envelope on the filter.

C3.C.q: Why is being told 'too long' or 'too short' enough to match a time?
options: The app shows the number after two tries
The ear judges times coarsely: double or half
Times barely change how a note sounds
Every hidden sound uses the same times
C3.C.why: The ear judges times coarsely, so within about double or half of the target counts as matched.
